New Orleans school closes early due to extreme heat
NEW ORLEANS —Students at Alice Harte Charter School in Algiers were sent home early after the air conditioning system failed, creating uncomfortably hot conditions in the classrooms.
"Our AC went out, and it was almost unlivable," one student said.
The incident comes just two weeks after students returned to the classroom on August 6.
School officials decided it was best to dismiss students early due to the high temperatures, which led many parents to leave work early to pick up their children.
"It was very hot in school, and my head started to hurt, and I almost got a heat flash," another student said.
"Were you happy you had to go home a little early?" a student was asked. "Yeah," the student replied.
Students were seen wearing their school sweaters despite the heat.
Maintenance crews are currently working on the equipment, and school officials said they anticipate reopening tomorrow.

Hot summer weather is no stranger to the Carolinas, but when the heat becomes extreme, it's a whole different story.
The National Weather Service will issue heat alerts when heat index, or "real-feel," numbers are forecast to reach 105 or higher and last for at least two hours.
A heat advisory is different from an extreme heat warning, depending on level of heat index forecast.
When heat warnings are issued, that often means the human body will likely see effects if caution, care and common sense are not taken.
Note the differences between heat exhaustion and heat stroke.
Heat exhaustion can be managed with basic care and adjustments, but heat stroke is serious and requires immediate medical attention.
Note the differences between heat exhaustion and heat stroke. Heat stroke is far more serious and requires immediate medial attention while heat exhaustion can be treated and managed on its own.
Meteorologists carefully monitor forecast temperatures, winds and humidity to determine if heat levels will pose a risk to health and safety.
When those numbers look to rise into those danger categories (orange and red), it's time to consider limiting normal outdoor activities, particularly those that are strenuous and last for multiple hours during the height of daylight hours (between noon and 6 p.m.).
The combination of heat and humidity determines the heat index - a number based upon how much harder the human body has to work to cool itself off to maintain safe, healthy core temperature.
Taking proper measures and planning accordingly can ensure a lesser chance of seeing those heat-related illnesses.
So be smart, be safe, use common sense and stay cool during those extremely hot summer days in the Carolinas!

New research reveals increasing health impact of heatwaves on over-60s – here’s why
A new study predicts rising global temperatures could have a greater health impact than previously thought on older adults. Harry Bullmore speaks to experts to find out how to ‘heat-proof’ as you get older
The study, published in The Lancet, investigated the potential impact of current climate projections on young (18-39), middle-aged (40-59) and older adults. The results suggest that “intolerable heat will be experienced at much larger scales and for longer durations, affecting far more people than previously estimated” – particularly among older adults.
The string of heatwaves in the UK this summer has gone some way to demonstrating the severity of this impact. But why are older adults at greater risk?
Why are older people at greater risk during heatwaves?
When we overheat, our body has to work harder to keep everything running smoothly. Dr Kim van Daalen, an environmental epidemiologist at the University of Cambridge, describes this as someone’s “adaptive capacity” – and she says it is usually lower in older people.
“We know that people who are older have less thermoregulatory efficiency [the ability to maintain a stable core body temperature],” she explains. “The same is true with very young children.”
Mobility is another factor to consider, particularly when considering climate events such as the recent wildfires in the UK.
“If someone is exposed to a wildfire and they are very mobile, they can reduce their exposure to it by going somewhere else,” says Dr van Daalen. “If someone is less mobile, they might not be able to adapt, so they will not be able to deal as well with the same environment and pollution.”
Older populations can also be at greater risk of dehydration, heat exhaustion and heat stroke, according to Professor Ron Maughan, honorary professor at the University of St Andrews’ School of Medicine. This can have serious repercussions on heart health.
“In hot weather, the consequences of dehydration are increased,” says Professor Maughan. “Your blood volume goes down when you’re dehydrated. If you have a lower blood volume, your heart needs to work harder to supply the blood to all the tissues that need it, so your heart rate goes up to compensate.
“The other thing that happens is, because the blood volume is reduced, the blood becomes a little bit thicker and stickier, and the heart has to work harder to push that blood through its capillaries. So staying well hydrated is important from a cardiovascular health point of view, particularly for older and less fit people.”
Dehydration can lead to lightheadedness, fatigue and dizziness. In the most serious cases, it can lead to fainting, coma and even prove fatal. But this last outcome is very rare, Professor Maughan says.
“The body’s defensive mechanisms are very good. They tend to stop us exercising if we’re in a situation where temperatures rise to dangerous levels.”
Fainting is one such mechanism that stops the body from moving or exercising before dehydration becomes too severe. There are other ways the body adapts to battle the heat too.
The most obvious thing you can do to avoid dehydration, heat exhaustion and heat stroke is to reduce your exposure to the heat.
“In heatwaves, we want to make sure we hydrate well and do not go outside or do intense physical activity during the hottest part of the day,” says Dr Van Daalen.
“Try to keep your home as cool as you can, which can be quite difficult in the UK because houses are designed to keep heat in. Keeping your curtains and windows closed when the air temperature is hotter than the inside temperature can help keep temperatures quite cool.
“And if you are experiencing symptoms of heat exhaustion, take steps to cool down as soon as possible.”
Symptoms of heat exhaustion include heavy sweating, light-headedness, a high heart rate, muscles cramps, weakness, lethargy and nausea, says Dr Linia Patel, a women’s health dietitian, performance nutritionist and public health researcher.
A key way to counter this, or prevent it from happening in the first place, is to stay hydrated throughout the day.
“Drink regularly throughout the day, rather than waiting until you feel thirsty,” Dr Patel advises. “Keep drinks cold if possible, as people tend to drink more when fluids are refreshing, and add slices of cucumber, orange, lemon or berries to water if it helps encourage intake.”
“To test your hydration levels, check your urine colour,’ she adds. “It should be the colour of pale straw. Dark yellow urine is often a sign you need more fluids as soon as possible.”
Professor Maughan was the lead author of a 2016 study which investigated various drinks for their hydrating properties. Perhaps surprisingly, he says water plays its part in hydration, but it is not “the ideal drink”.
“Fruit juices are not bad. Milk is also not bad as it contains a bit of salt. But the sensible thing is to aim for a variety of drinks in moderation,” he says.
“When you sweat, you lose salt, and water doesn’t contain salt. Think about the sports drinks we give to athletes when they’re working hard in the heat. They contain a bit of sugar, a bit of salt and some water.
“Salt is important. It acts like a sponge and holds water in the body. If you drink plain water it dilutes the body’s fluids, sending a message to the brain and the kidneys that you’re over-hydrated and you need to pee.”
This doesn’t mean you need to invest in an expensive electrolyte supplement, though. These can be useful for athletes in “extreme situations” such as lengthy endurance challenges, but for the average person, an intuitive change in diet can work wonders.
“When you get thirsty, your taste for salt increases,” Professor Maughan says. “You’ll tend to naturally build a little bit more salt into what you eat. So [for most people] there isn’t much difference between taking a fancy formulated drink and having water and a pizza.”
The individuality of hydration
While the general advice is that we need eight glasses of water a day, a 2022 study from the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the US found this may be a myth. Researchers measured the water intake of over 5,000 people from 26 countries, ranging in age from babies to 96-year-olds, and found the amount of water needed to stay healthy varied considerably.
Elite athletes have tests available to learn more about their requirements. For the rest of us, other signs can inform our hydration habits.
“If you weigh yourself before a training run and you weigh 70kg, then you weigh yourself after, and your bodyweight is down by a kilo, you’ve lost about 1.4 per cent of your bodyweight – that’s OK,” says Professor Maughan. “If you’d lost two kilos, you would need to drink a little bit more.
“As for salt: if you wear a black T-shirt when you’re exercising and you see those white patches crusted under the armpits, you are a salty sweater. About one in eight of the people we studied produced a lot of salt in their sweat, so they need to pay more attention to replacing that.
“They’ll naturally tend to reach for the salt shaker and put a little bit more salt on their food. It’s not necessarily a conscious response.”
Men are generally larger, so they will need to replace more fluid on a daily basis than smaller women. Any cause of fluid loss from the body, including menstruation, will increase the fluid requirements.
In most cases the body will indicate an individual’s hydration needs, but some elderly people may have an impaired thirst mechanism and need to be encouraged to drink more than their thirst directs. Especially when elderly adults may also be on medications that increase urine output, which means they will need to be more cautious.

title: Extreme heat calls for preparation - The Brewton Standard
search_term: (heatstroke OR "heat stroke" OR sunstroke OR "heat exhaustion" OR "heat-related death" OR "heat casualty" OR "heat fatality" OR "suspected heat death" OR dehydration OR "heat cramps" OR "heat illness") Assam
full_text:
Heat cramps – include muscle pains or spasms (abdomen, arms or legs), profuse sweat, and high salt concentration in the sweat.
Heat exhaustion – is associated with heavy sweating, paleness, muscle cramps, tiredness, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea, or vomiting and fainting. Other possible symptoms may include cool and moist skin, a fast and weak pulse rate, fast and shallow breathing, or irritability. Older adults, those with high blood pressure, and those working or exercising in a hot environment are prone to heat exhaustion. If heat exhaustion is not treated, it may progress to heatstroke.
Heat stroke or sun stroke – the most serious heat-related illness, a life-threatening problem, may occur when the body is unable to control its temperature. Body temperature may rise to 106 degrees F or higher within 10 -15 minutes. Signs include an extremely high body temperature, red, hot and dry or moist skin, rapid, strong pulse, throbbing headache, dizziness, nausea, dehydration, combativeness or confusion, and unconsciousness. Heat stroke is a medical emergency and even with immediate treatment, it can be life-threatening or cause serious long-term problems.
Recommendations are that people drink plenty of fluids and avoid alcohol or caffeinated beverages to prevent dehydration, stay in an air-conditioned room, keep out of the sun by seeking shelter, wear a wide-brimmed hat, light-colored and loose-fitting clothing, use sunscreen of SPF 15 or higher, take cool showers or baths, and reduce or eliminate strenuous activities during the hottest times of the day. NEVER leave people or pets in a parked vehicle.
Individuals with heart disease, diabetes, obesity, poor circulation, or a history of stroke, people of older and younger ages, and those taking certain medications are at high risk of becoming ill in hot weather.
For more information, visit https://www.alabamapublichealth.gov/injuryprevention/heat.html
